To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
granulocyte transfusion therapy may have a beneficial effect in patients with neutropenic infections, but further study is required.

(a) granulocyte transfusion therapy is effective for patients with severe neutropenia and infections, (b) granulocyte and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factors (CSF) are effective in increasing granulocyte production and function, (c) the optimal dose of granulocytes to be transfused has not yet been determined, (d) granulocyte-mobilizing agents such as cyclophosphamide and etoposide are effective

granulocyte and/or platelet transfusions are not efficacious as prophylaxis in neutropenic cancer patients but may be effective as therapy in selected patients with infections refractory to appropriate antibiotic therapy and with low peripheral granulocyte counts.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: (1) the development of improved methods for the collection of granulocytes by leukapheresis, (2) the development of more effective methods for the cryopreservation of leukocytes, and (3) the development of better methods of evaluating the clinical effectiveness of granulocyte support in patients with acute leukemia.

the evaluation of granulocyte, platelet, and lymphocyte products obtained by leukapheresis, plateletpheresis, and lymphopheresis, and the development of improved methods of obtaining, storing, and using these products.
the development and application of improved procedures for the collection, processing, storage, and transfusion of granulocytes, platelets, and other components of whole blood.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of leukapheresis or plateletpheresis in the management of patients with cancer remains an experimental procedure.
the current status of leukocyte or platelet administration in the treatment of cancer remains uncertain.
leukocyte and platelets are of great potential value in the support of patients with cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

granulocyte and/or platelet support is a valuable adjunct to the treatment of patients with neutropenia and/or thrombocytopenia, especially when used in conjunction with aggressive antimicrobial and supportive care, and that the risks and benefits of such therapy must be considered on a patient by patient basis.
leukocyte and platelets transfusions are not as effective as they might be, but they are still useful.
the use of granulocyte or platelet apheresis in the treatment of cancer is not yet a standard of therapy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the current use of leukapheresis in cancer therapy is limited and the indications for plateletpheresis in this setting are not yet clearly defined.
the best approach is to avoid the use of granulocyte or platelet transfusions whenever possible.

the use of leukapheresis products is still limited, but the use of plateletpheresis products is increasing, and that the future of leukapheresed products is in cryopreserved granulocytes and in the use of leukocytes in the treatment of cancer.
